notes.h: What striking and fielding games share
notes.b: Cricket, softball and rounders look different, but they are built the same way: one side tries to score while the other tries to stop them. Knowing this shared structure helps you make sense of every skill that follows.
points: One team bats (hits the ball with a bat) to score runs, or rounders in rounders, while the other team bowls or pitches (delivers the ball to the batter) and fields (catches and retrieves the ball) to stop runs and get batters out.
Each team bats in an innings (the turn a team takes at batting), after which the teams swap roles, so both sides get to bat and to bowl and field.
notes.tip: Striking and fielding games are used in exams for skill analysis, decision-making, levers (batting) and teamwork, so be ready to link each skill to one of these.

notes.b: Every cricket shot starts from a good set-up. A balanced stance and a correct grip give the batter control of the bat before the ball arrives.
points: Stance: stand side-on to the bowler, with feet shoulder-width apart, so you are balanced and can move forwards or back, and keep the head still and the eyes level so you can judge the ball.
Grip: hold the bat with the hands together at the top of the handle, so the two hands work as one unit when you swing.
notes.tip: Exams use these games for skill analysis and levers (batting), so describe stance and grip point by point and say what each contributes to the shot.

notes.h: Cricket drives, cut, pull and glance
notes.b: A batter chooses the shot according to the ball. Full balls (which pitch close to the batter) are driven; shorter balls (which pitch further from the batter) call for back-foot shots, the cut, the pull or the glance.
points: Drives (straight, on and off, named for the direction the ball is hit) are played to a full ball with a front-foot step towards the ball.
Front-foot drive: keep the head over the ball, the elbow high, and finish with a straight bat follow-through so the ball is hit along the intended line.
Back-foot shots are played to shorter balls, with the weight moved back rather than forward.
Cut: played square (at a right angle to the pitch) on the off side (the side the bat faces in the stance) to a short, wide ball.
Pull: a horizontal bat swung at a short ball on the leg side (the side of the batter's body behind the legs).
Glance: deflects the ball finely on the leg side, meaning it is turned away to the area behind the batter rather than hit hard.
notes.tip: When asked to analyse a shot, state which ball it is played to (full, short, wide) and then the body and bat positions, because the choice of shot depends on the ball.

notes.b: A bowling action is a chain of linked movements. Each stage builds speed and balance for the next, ending with a legal release of the ball.
points: Action in order: 1. run-up, 2. gather (bringing the body together ready to deliver), 3. side-on or front-on delivery stride, 4. release, 5. follow-through.
The bowling arm must be straight, with no throwing, because throwing is not a legal delivery.
In cricket the bowling arm must not straighten during delivery (throwing is illegal).
notes.tip: The trap here is the arm. In cricket the bowling arm must not straighten during delivery, because throwing is illegal, so never describe a bent-then-straightened arm as correct.

notes.h: Line, length and types of delivery
notes.b: Bowlers try to make batting difficult by controlling where the ball pitches (lands) and how it moves after that. Line, length and the type of delivery are the three tools they use.
points: Line (the direction of the ball): aim at or just outside off stump (the stump nearest the off side, part of the wicket the batter defends).
Good length: makes the batter unsure whether to go forward or back, so they are more likely to choose the wrong shot.
Medium and fast pace: bowling that uses seam and swing (the stitched ridge of the ball and its movement through the air).
Spin: off-spin and leg-spin, which turn the ball off the pitch, so the ball changes direction after it lands.
notes.tip: Use line and length together in answers, for example at or just outside off stump on a good length, and name the type of delivery as pace (seam and swing) or spin.

notes.b: Fielders are placed close to the bat to catch edges and far away near the boundary to stop runs. The skills differ because the ball arrives in different ways.
points: Close fielding (slips, short leg, positions near the batter): stay low and ready, with soft hands, because the ball arrives quickly and may be an edge.
Deep fielding (boundary, the edge of the playing area): take a long barrier (a position with the body and legs behind the ball) to stop the ball.
Deep fielding: attack the ball and make a flat throw to the keeper (the wicketkeeper, who stands behind the stumps).
notes.tip: Striking and fielding games are used for teamwork and decision-making, so link fielding to team roles, for example a flat throw to the keeper.

notes.h: Catching and throwing in softball and rounders
notes.b: Catching and throwing are the basic skills of the fielding side in softball and rounders. A good catch gets a batter out, and an accurate throw stops runs.
points: Catching: use two hands, with the hands forming a cup or basket, and give with the ball (let the hands move back with it) so it does not bounce out.
Throwing: throw overarm from a side-on stance, stepping towards the target so the body weight goes in the direction of the throw.

notes.b: Hitting (also called striking or batting) is how the batting side starts a run. A controlled swing sends the ball into space and gives the batter time to run.
points: Stance: side-on, with the eyes on the ball so you can time the contact.
Swing: level through the ball, with a full follow-through.
After the hit, the batter runs to the next post or base (the marked points the batter must reach).
Drop the bat (do not throw it) before running.
notes.tip: Levers (batting) are a listed exam context, so describe the swing and follow-through in order.

notes.h: Pitching and bowling in softball and rounders
notes.b: Pitching or bowling puts the ball into play. The rules about how the ball is delivered differ between the games, so know which applies.
points: Rounders bowling is underarm, meaning the arm swings from below the shoulder.
In rounders the ball must pass between the batter's head and knee on the batting side, so that it is a fair delivery the batter can hit.
Variations: pace (speed), swerve (curving through the air) and spin.
Line and length: the ball is pitched to a consistent line and length so the batter cannot predict it.
notes.tip: Remember that rounders bowling is underarm, and that a good ball passes between the batter's head and knee on the batting side.

notes.h: Fielding positions in softball and rounders
notes.b: Fielders are spread across the pitch so that every area is covered. Their positions have names, and each job helps the team stop the batter scoring.
points: Rounders positions: backstop (behind the batter), bowler, and first to fourth post fielders (one at each post).
Softball positions: basemen (fielders who guard each base), with deep fielders covering the outfield (the area far from the batter).
Fielding on base: stretch to catch the ball with a foot on the base, so the runner is out as soon as the ball arrives.
Deep fielders back up: move behind the fielder throwing the ball, so that a missed or overthrown ball can be stopped.
notes.tip: Backing up is a good example of teamwork, so use it when an answer asks how fielders help each other.

notes.b: Cricket scoring is in runs, and the fielding side gets a batter out by one of several dismissals. These rules decide what the skills are for.
points: Runs: batters run between the wickets (the sets of stumps at each end of the pitch) to score.
Boundaries: 4 runs when the ball crosses the boundary along the ground, and 6 when it crosses on the full (without bouncing).

Dismissals: bowled (the ball hits the stumps), caught (a fielder catches it before it bounces), run out, LBW (leg before wicket, when the batter's body blocks a ball that would hit the stumps) and stumped (the keeper removes the bails when the batter is out of the crease).

notes.b: Rounders and softball each have their own scoring and out rules. Learn them separately, because the same word can mean different things.
points: Rounders: a rounder is scored by reaching fourth post.
Rounders: a batter is out if caught, if a post is stumped before they reach it, or if they overtake another batter.
Softball: runs are scored for reaching home.
Softball: three outs end the innings, after which the teams swap roles.
notes.tip: Remember that in rounders the score is a rounder, earned by reaching fourth post.

notes.b: Tactics are the decisions a team makes to gain an advantage. Both sides use them, so exam answers can look at batting and at fielding.
points: Batting into gaps: placing the ball where fielders cannot reach it, so runs can be taken safely.
Running calls between wickets or posts: yes, no or wait, so both batters know whether to run.
Fielding placement is set for the batter and for the bowler, so fielders cover the likely shots.
Bowling to the field that has been set, so the delivery and the fielders work together.
notes.tip: Decision-making and teamwork are the exam contexts for these games, so give each tactic with its reason.

notes.h: Safety in striking and fielding games
notes.b: A hard ball travelling at speed can cause injury, so these games depend on equipment and safe habits.
points: Cricket protective equipment: helmet, pads, gloves and box.
A hard ball creates a danger zone, so players must stay alert to where it is travelling.
Batters drop the bat, never throw it, so no one nearby is hit.
Fielders call for catches so that team-mates do not collide.

keyTerms.definition: A team's turn to bat, after which the teams swap roles.
A drive in which the batter steps the front foot towards a full ball, keeping the head over it.
A square shot on the off side played to a short, wide ball.
A horizontal-bat shot played to a short ball on the leg side.
A shot that deflects the ball finely on the leg side.
The direction of the bowler's delivery, aimed at or just outside off stump.
How far down the pitch the ball lands, with a good length making the batter unsure whether to go forward or back.
The edge of the cricket field, where a ball that reaches it scores 4 or 6.
A way of getting a batter out, such as bowled, caught, run out, LBW or stumped.
The score in rounders gained by a batter who reaches fourth post.
The rounders fielder positioned behind the batter.
Softball fielders who guard the bases.
Moving behind a fielder who is throwing, so that a missed or overthrown ball can be stopped.

questions.prompt: Describe the front-foot drive in cricket and explain how line and length affect the batter's choice of shot.
questions.model: Front-foot drive: the batter steps the front foot towards the pitch of a full ball, keeps the head over the ball with the eyes on it, and drives with a high elbow, finishing with a straight bat follow-through. Line and length: the bowler aims at or just outside off stump, which is the line the batter must judge. A good length makes the batter unsure whether to go forward or back, so the batter has to read the length early. A full ball suits the front-foot drive, while a shorter ball calls for a back-foot shot such as the cut, pull or glance.

questions.prompt: Describe how to catch and throw a ball in rounders or softball.
questions.model: Catch: use two hands, with the hands forming a cup or basket, and give with the ball as it arrives so that it is cushioned. Throw: use an overarm throw from a side-on stance, stepping towards the target as the ball is released.
